meta.titre: Urban Climate and the Heat Island: why built-up areas are warmer
meta.sous_theme: Causes, effects and management of the urban heat island

sections.contenu_markdown: On a calm, clear evening in a large city such as Douala or Yaounde, walls and tarred roads go on giving out heat long after sunset, while open farmland outside the city cools much faster. The built-up area is a warmer island in a cooler rural sea, and this is called the urban heat island. Cities in Cameroon and across Africa are growing quickly, so the topic matters for health, energy use and planning. GCE examiners ask especially for the ways in which people are responsible. A strong answer names each cause, explains the physical process and states the effect on temperature.

items: Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight than light surfaces, which reflect more.
Evaporation and transpiration use heat energy and so cool the surface.
The Earth's surface gives out heat as long-wave radiation, especially at night.
A temperature difference is found by subtracting one temperature from the other.

sections.titre: The urban heat island: causes, effects and management
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What it is
The urban heat island (UHI) is the higher air temperature of a built-up area compared with the surrounding countryside. It is strongest at night, a few hours after sunset, when the sky is clear and the air is calm, because rural surfaces cool quickly while the city releases stored heat. The **UHI intensity** is the urban temperature minus the rural temperature, often a few degrees Celsius in large cities.

### Causes (all linked to human land use)
| Cause | Process |
|---|---|
| Surface materials | Concrete, tarmac, bricks and metal roofs absorb a large share of sunshine (low albedo) and store heat by day, then release it at night. |
| Urban geometry | Tall buildings and narrow streets trap radiation by repeated reflection, reduce the amount of sky from which heat can escape and slow the wind that would remove heat. |
| Less vegetation and water | Fewer plants and open water mean less evaporation and transpiration, so more of the energy heats the air; drains remove rainwater quickly. |
| Human heat | Vehicles, factories, power stations, air conditioners, cooking and lighting release heat directly. |
| Air pollution | Dust, smoke and gases form a pollution dome that absorbs and returns some of the heat leaving the surface. |

### Other climate differences
Compared with the countryside a city usually has lower relative humidity, lower average wind speed (though gusty between buildings), more pollution and often more convective rain and storms over or downwind of the city.

### Effects and management
Effects are higher demand for cooling and electricity, heat stress and illness (especially for the elderly and young children), and worse air quality. Management includes green roofs, urban trees and parks, light-coloured and reflective roofs, permeable paving, water features, wider streets and open corridors that let wind through, public transport and energy-efficient buildings.

### Measurement
Readings from thermometers along a transect from the rural edge to the centre show a sharp rise (the "cliff") at the city edge, a gentler rise over the suburbs (the "plateau") and the highest values in the dense centre (the "peak").

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how people are responsible, or for a stated number of causes.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use three links for each cause: the human action (building with concrete and tarmac), the process (more sunlight absorbed and stored, less evaporation) and the effect (higher night temperature). Choose exactly the number of causes requested and develop each fully.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how urban climate differs from rural climate.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use a table with matching rows for temperature, humidity, wind, rain and air quality, and give the reason for each difference, for example that humidity is lower in the city because surfaces drain water away and there are fewer plants.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to compare absorbed energy for different surfaces.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Albedo is the fraction of incoming radiation that is reflected. The fraction absorbed is one minus the albedo, so absorbed energy is incoming radiation multiplied by $(1 - \text{albedo})$. Dark surfaces have low albedo and absorb more.

sections.enonce_markdown:
At 10 pm the air temperature is 29.4 degrees Celsius in the centre of a large tropical city and 25.1 degrees Celsius in nearby farmland. At noon the incoming solar radiation is 800 watts per square metre. Assume tarmac has an albedo of 0.10 and grass has an albedo of 0.25.

(a) Calculate the UHI intensity.
(b) Calculate the energy absorbed per square metre by each surface.
(c) Explain two ways in which human activities cause the heat island. (10 marks)

etapes.justification: It is the urban temperature minus the rural temperature at the same time.

etapes.action: Calculate the absorbed energy for tarmac.
etapes.justification: Absorbed energy equals incoming radiation multiplied by (1 minus albedo).

etapes.action: Calculate the absorbed energy for grass.
etapes.justification: Use the same method so that the two surfaces can be compared.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $800 \times (1 - 0.25) = 600\ \mathrm{W\ m^{-2}}$, so tarmac absorbs 120 $\mathrm{W\ m^{-2}}$ more

etapes.action: Explain the first human cause: replacing vegetated land with concrete and tarmac.
etapes.justification: Link the action to the process and to the temperature effect.
etapes.resultat_markdown: People cover the ground with materials of low albedo that absorb more sunshine and store it. At night they give the heat back slowly, so the city stays warmer than farmland. Removing plants and filling the surface with drains also reduces evaporation and transpiration, so less energy goes into cooling and more heats the air.

etapes.action: Explain the second human cause: heat and pollution released by activity.
etapes.justification: Name a source, say how it adds heat and state its effect.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Vehicles, factories, generators, cooking fires and air conditioners release heat into the streets. Smoke, dust and exhaust gases form a pollution dome that absorbs and returns part of the heat leaving the surface, which reduces night cooling.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The UHI intensity is **4.3 degrees Celsius**. Tarmac absorbs **720 W m$^{-2}$** and grass **600 W m$^{-2}$**, a difference of **120 W m$^{-2}$**. Human responsibility lies in the materials and design of the built environment, the removal of vegetation, and the heat and pollution released by activity.

items.erreur_markdown: "The urban heat island is caused by global warming."
items.pourquoi_faux: The heat island is a local effect caused by the form and activities of the city. Global warming is a worldwide change, and the two can add to each other but are different.
items.correction_markdown: Explain the heat island by local factors such as surface materials, loss of vegetation and human heat.

items.erreur_markdown: "Cities are always hotter than the countryside by the same amount."
items.pourquoi_faux: The effect is strongest at night with clear, calm weather. It becomes weak in windy, cloudy conditions and by day.
items.correction_markdown: State when the effect is strongest and that its size changes with weather and city size.

items.erreur_markdown: "Cars and factories cause the heat island." (no process given)
items.pourquoi_faux: A cause without a process earns little. The examiner wants to know how they raise temperature.
items.correction_markdown: Explain that vehicles and factories release heat directly, and that their pollution absorbs outgoing heat, reducing night cooling.

items.pourquoi_faux: Concrete does not create heat. It absorbs and stores solar energy during the day and releases it slowly.
items.correction_markdown: Write that concrete and tarmac absorb and store heat by day and release it at night.

items.enonce_markdown: Temperatures at 11 pm are: rural farm 25.0, suburb 26.8, inner city 28.9 and central business district (CBD) 30.2 degrees Celsius. (a) Calculate the UHI intensity for each urban station. (b) Name the part of the city where the temperature peaks.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Suburb: $26.8 - 25.0 = $ **1.8 degrees Celsius**; inner city: $28.9 - 25.0 = $ **3.9 degrees Celsius**; CBD: $30.2 - 25.0 = $ **5.2 degrees Celsius**.
(b) The peak is in the **CBD**, where buildings are densest, vegetation is least and human heat is greatest.

items.enonce_markdown: A school in a hot city replaces an old roof of albedo 0.15 with a white-painted roof of albedo 0.60. Take the incoming radiation as 900 watts per square metre. (a) Calculate the energy absorbed per square metre by each roof. (b) Calculate the percentage reduction in absorbed energy. (c) Explain how large numbers of such roofs could reduce the heat island.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Old roof: $900 \times (1 - 0.15) = $ **765 W m$^{-2}$**. New roof: $900 \times (1 - 0.60) = $ **360 W m$^{-2}$**.
(b) Reduction $= 765 - 360 = 405$ W m$^{-2}$, so $\frac{405}{765} \times 100 = $ **52.9%**.
(c) Light roofs reflect more sunshine and absorb and store less heat, so less heat is released to the air at night; spread over many buildings, the average temperature of the city falls and less energy is needed for cooling.

items.enonce_markdown: A city council wants to reduce its heat island. Suggest and evaluate three measures, and say which one you would put first.
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for three measures, each explained and evaluated, for example: **urban trees and parks** (shade and transpiration cool the air; also improve air quality and health; need land, water and care); **reflective roofs and light-coloured paving** (raise albedo, cheap and quick; may increase glare and need repainting); **green roofs and permeable surfaces** (add evaporation and absorb rainwater; costly to install on old buildings); **planning for ventilation** (wide streets or corridors let wind remove heat; needs land and long-term planning); **public transport and efficient buildings** (cut human heat; need investment). Reward a justified priority, such as trees and parks first because they cool, shade and improve health at a moderate cost.

items_markdown: The urban heat island is the warmer air of a built-up area compared with the countryside; it is strongest at night under clear, calm skies. Intensity = urban temperature minus rural temperature.

Causes: low-albedo, heat-storing surfaces; building geometry that traps heat and slows wind; fewer plants and less evaporation; heat from traffic, industry and air conditioning; air pollution that returns heat.
The city also tends to have lower relative humidity, lower mean wind speed, more pollution and often more convective rain.
Effects: higher cooling demand, heat stress and poorer air quality. Management: trees and parks, reflective and green roofs, permeable surfaces, ventilation corridors and less human heat.
In answers for each cause give the human action, the process and the temperature effect, and in calculations show the formula, substitution and unit.
